title: Common Machine Learning Algorithms
learning_outcomes: Explain common Machine Learning Algorithms and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.
Apply the central idea in common Machine Learning Algorithms to a small example or select a suitable approach for a stated scenario.
Identify an important assumption, failure mode, risk, or limitation and describe how it should be checked.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study common Machine Learning Algorithms within Machine Learning Fundamentals. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Machine learning estimates patterns from examples. Define the task, select a meaningful baseline, and reserve unseen data for honest evaluation.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Algorithms make different assumptions about relationships, distances, interactions, and noise. There is no universally best algorithm; compare candidates empirically while avoiding leakage and excessive tuning to the test set.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: Linear regression
items.text: Linear regression predicts a numeric target using a weighted combination of input features. Inspect residuals, units, feature relationships, and assumptions before treating coefficients as meaningful explanations.

items.title: Logistic regression
items.text: Despite its name, logistic regression is commonly used for classification by mapping a linear score to an estimated probability. Calibration, feature scaling, thresholds, and class balance influence its practical use.

items.title: Decision trees
items.text: A decision tree recursively splits examples using feature-based rules. Shallow trees are easy to inspect, while deep trees may memorize training cases; validate depth and leaf-size choices.

items.title: Random forests
items.text: A random forest combines many decision trees trained with randomness in samples and features. Aggregation can improve stability, but interpretation, latency, and calibration still need checking.

items.title: Gradient-boosted trees
items.text: Boosting builds a sequence of learners that focus on residual patterns or errors from earlier stages. Tune depth, learning rate, and number of stages using validation data.

items.title: Support vector machines
items.text: Support vector machines choose a boundary based on margin and may use kernels for nonlinear separation. Scaling and the choice of kernel and regularization parameter affect results.

items.title: k-nearest neighbors
items.text: Nearest-neighbor methods predict from examples close under a chosen distance function. Feature scales, irrelevant variables, neighborhood size, and inference cost can strongly affect performance.

items.title: Naive Bayes
items.text: Bayes’ theorem updates a prior belief using the likelihood of observed evidence to compute a posterior. Be explicit about the event, evidence, and base rate; a high likelihood ratio does not erase a very small prior probability.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Identify what common machine learning algorithms takes as input and what result or decision it is intended to support. 2. Read the example before running it and predict the output. 3. Run the small example, compare actual and expected output, then change one input or assumption and repeat. 4. Record what the example demonstrates and what it does not demonstrate about a real system.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with the task definition and the inputs available. Make the expected behavior explicit, choose a simple reference point, and inspect both ordinary examples and cases where assumptions may fail. Machine learning estimates patterns from examples. Define the task, select a meaningful baseline, and reserve unseen data for honest evaluation.

content_blocks.code:
train = [0, 1, 1, 0]
validation = [0, 1]
baseline_prediction = max(set(train), key=train.count)
accuracy = sum(baseline_prediction == y for y in validation) / len(validation)
print("baseline accuracy:", round(accuracy, 2))
content_blocks.run_instructions: Copy the code into a local file named main.py and run `python main.py` with Python 3. Compare the printed output with the expected result documented here. This CodeLeaf content block is static; it does not execute the snippet in the browser and needs no external API key.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet or return to the small synthetic input, rerun it, and change one value at a time. Do not add real credentials, private user data, or untrusted code to the example.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Algorithms make different assumptions about relationships, distances, interactions, and noise. There is no universally best algorithm; compare candidates empirically while avoiding leakage and excessive tuning to the test set. Next, connect this lesson to its prerequisite or next lesson and carry the same habit forward: define success, test a representative case, inspect failures, and document limitations.

content.task: Try it yourself: build a tiny synthetic dataset for common machine learning algorithms, establish a simple baseline, and define a suitable metric before looking at results. Separate development decisions from final evaluation and describe one important error. The linked practice activity is: Compare ML Algorithms.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core concept and accurately refer to the source syllabus topics.
Record a prediction and compare it with a reproducible result or a clearly stated manual trace.
Document at least one limitation, safety consideration, or evaluation requirement.
hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
troubleshooting: Use Python 3 and run the file from the folder where it was saved.
If output differs, restore the original input and compare one changed value at a time.
If Python reports a syntax error, check copied quotation marks, indentation, and whether the full code block was copied.
These examples require no external packages, network access, model credentials, or personal data.
